# What we are *not* doing today

.pull-left-small2[
## Ground already covered

- The **grammar of graphics** and **ggplot2 basics** ([Session 8 / IDS-25](https://raw.githack.com/intro-to-data-science-25/lectures/main/08-visualization/08-visualization.html))
- **Chart types** and when to use each ([FT Visual Vocabulary](https://ft-interactive.github.io/visual-vocabulary/); [Claus Wilke's Fundamentals of Data Visualization](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/))
- **Cleveland/Tufte** principles: data-ink, proportional ink, comparison, etc. ([Session 8 / IDS-25](https://raw.githack.com/intro-to-data-science-25/lectures/main/08-visualization/08-visualization.html))
- Most of the science of **communicating uncertainty** ([Session 3](https://raw.githack.com/data-journalism-26/slides/main/03-how-people-understand-numbers/03-how-people-understand-numbers.html))
- **Basic ingredients** of data visualization, such as colors, line and plot types, etc. ([Session 8 / IDS-25](https://raw.githack.com/intro-to-data-science-25/lectures/main/08-visualization/08-visualization.html#60))

Instead, we will spend the session on the things that
separate an analyst's chart from a published one.
]

.pull-right-wide2[
## Dos and Don'ts (click links for background)

1. [Follow the principle of proportional ink.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/proportional-ink.html)
2. [Maximize the data–ink ratio, within reason.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/balance-data-context.html)
3. [Avoid invisible overplotting.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/overlapping-points.html)
4. [Drop all the unimportant stuff.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/balance-data-context.html)
5. [Don't overload graphs. Instead, use several.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/multi-panel-figures.html)
6. [Use color scales that match the logic of the data scale.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/color-pitfalls.html)
7. [Use color-vision deficient-friendly colors.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/color-pitfalls.html#not-designing-for-color-vision-deficiency)
8. [Only use a legend when you need one.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/redundant-coding.html#designing-figures-without-legends)
9. [Pay attention to legend order.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/figure-titles-captions.html#axis-and-legend-titles)
10. [Label axes properly (but avoid trivial information).](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/figure-titles-captions.html#figure-titles-and-captions)
11. [Use grids and helper lines, within reason.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/balance-data-context.html#background-grids)
12. [Don't order alphabetically ("Alabama first"). Use natural orders instead.](https://datajournalism.com/read/longreads/the-unspoken-rules-of-visualisation)
13. [Bar chart axes should include zero.](https://datajournalism.com/read/longreads/the-unspoken-rules-of-visualisation)
14. [Put the explanatory variable on the x axis, the outcome on the y axis.](https://datajournalism.com/read/longreads/the-unspoken-rules-of-visualisation)
15. [Axes have canonical directions. Larger values are placed above/right of smaller values.](https://datajournalism.com/read/longreads/the-unspoken-rules-of-visualisation)
16. [Avoid multiple y axes at all cost.](https://blog.datawrapper.de/dualaxis/)
17. [Don't do pie charts. (Or maybe do?)](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-proportions.html)
18. [Don't go 3D.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/no-3d.html)
19. [Use readable fonts and font sizes.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/small-axis-labels.html)
20. [Sometimes a table is just enough.](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/figure-titles-captions.html#figure-titles-and-captions)
]

# The science of annotations

.pull-left[
**Borkin et al. (2016)** — eye-tracked readers across ~400 charts.
What they remembered most was the **title and text**, not the
encoding. [*IEEE TVCG*](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7192646) ·
[PDF](http://olivalab.mit.edu/Papers/07192646.pdf)

**Kong, Liu & Karahalios (2018)** — same chart, different titles.
A title that slants toward one interpretation **shifts what readers
take away**, even when the data is identical. A misaligned title can
override the perception entirely.
[*ACM CHI*](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3173574.3174012) ·
[PDF](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3173574.3174012)

**Hullman & Diakopoulos (2011)** — frames annotation as one of
**four editorial layers** (data, representation, annotation,
interactivity). The annotation layer is *where rhetoric lives*, and
where it is most often denied.
[*IEEE TVCG*](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6064988) ·
[PDF](https://users.eecs.northwestern.edu/~jhullman/vis_rhetoric.pdf)
]

.pull-right[
<div align="center">
<br>
<img src="pics/borkin-abstract.png" style="width:100%; height:auto;">
</div>

`Source` [Borkin et al. (2016)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7192646)
]

> The words on a chart aren't decoration — they *are* the message that is most likely to be remembered.

# Guess the outlet!

```{r embed-outlet-data, echo=FALSE, results='asis', message=FALSE}
# Bake the contents of app/ (PNG/JPG screenshots of charts from various outlets)
# into the HTML at knit time, so the slide is self-contained.
# Convention: outlet key = everything before the first "-" or "_" in the
# filename, e.g.
#   ft.png            -> "ft"
#   ft-1.png          -> "ft"
#   ft_burnmurdoch.png-> "ft"
#   nyt-upshot.png    -> "nyt"
# Drop multiple files per outlet to enlarge the deck.
.og_dir   <- "app"
.og_files <- if (dir.exists(.og_dir)) {
  list.files(.og_dir, pattern = "\\.(png|jpe?g|gif)$",
             ignore.case = TRUE, full.names = FALSE)
} else character()

# Display labels for known outlet keys; unknown keys fall back to title-case.
.og_labels <- c(
  bild      = "Bild",
  economist = "The Economist",
  ft        = "Financial Times",
  guardian  = "The Guardian",
  nyt       = "New York Times",
  reuters   = "Reuters",
  spiegel   = "Der Spiegel",
  sz        = "Süddeutsche Zeitung",
  taz       = "taz",
  wapo      = "Washington Post",
  zeit      = "Die Zeit",
  owid      = "Our World in Data",
  pew      = "Pew Research Center",
  ard      = "ARD",
  zdf      = "ZDF",
  fivethirtyeight = "FiveThirtyEight"
)
.og_titlecase <- function(x) {
  paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substr(x, 2, nchar(x)))
}

if (length(.og_files)) {
  .og_keys <- tolower(sub("[-_].*$", "",
                          tools::file_path_sans_ext(.og_files)))
  .og_items <- data.frame(
    img = file.path(.og_dir, .og_files),
    k   = .og_keys,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  .og_unique <- sort(unique(.og_keys))
  .og_outlets <- data.frame(
    k     = .og_unique,
    label = ifelse(.og_unique %in% names(.og_labels),
                   .og_labels[.og_unique],
                   .og_titlecase(.og_unique)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  .og_payload <- jsonlite::toJSON(
    list(items = .og_items, outlets = .og_outlets),
    dataframe = "rows", auto_unbox = TRUE
  )
  .og_payload <- gsub("</", "<\\/", .og_payload, fixed = TRUE)
  cat('<script>window.OG_DATA = ', .og_payload, ';</script>', sep = "")
} else {
  cat('<script>window.OG_DATA = {items:[], outlets:[]};</script>')
}
```

<div id="og" style="max-width:880px; margin:6px auto; font-family:inherit;">
  <div id="og-score" style="text-align:right; color:#888; font-size:14px;">Score: 0 / 0</div>
  <div id="og-card" style="background:#fff; border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:12px;
       padding:14px; min-height:360px; box-shadow:0 4px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.08);
       margin-top:6px; display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;">
    <img id="og-img" src="" alt="" style="max-height:340px; max-width:100%;
         object-fit:contain; display:none;">
    <span id="og-msg" style="font-size:18px; color:#666;">Loading…</span>
  </div>
  <div id="og-buttons" style="display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; justify-content:center;
       gap:10px; margin-top:12px;"></div>
  <div id="og-feedback" style="min-height:30px; margin-top:10px; text-align:center;
       font-size:16px;"></div>
</div>

<script>
(function () {
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);

  function shuffle(a) {
    for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
      const j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1));
      [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]];
    }
    return a;
  }

  const data    = window.OG_DATA || {items: [], outlets: []};
  let items     = (data.items   || []).slice();
  const outlets = (data.outlets || []).slice();

  let i = 0, right = 0, total = 0, locked = false;

  function labelFor(k) {
    const o = outlets.find(o => o.k === k);
    return o ? o.label : k;
  }

  function renderButtons() {
    // Inline onclick handlers survive remark.js re-parsing of slide HTML;
    // addEventListener attached on the original DOM does not.
    $('og-buttons').innerHTML = outlets.map(o =>
      '<button onclick="window.ogGuess(\'' + o.k + '\')" ' +
      'style="padding:10px 18px; border:none; border-radius:8px; ' +
      'background:#1D375B; color:#fff; cursor:pointer; font-size:14px;">' +
      o.label + '</button>'
    ).join('');
  }

  function setButtonsDisabled(state) {
    $('og-buttons').querySelectorAll('button').forEach(b => b.disabled = state);
  }

  function render() {
    if (i >= items.length) {
      $('og-img').style.display = 'none';
      $('og-msg').style.display = 'block';
      $('og-msg').innerHTML =
        '<b>Done!</b><br><span style="font-size:16px; color:#666;">Final score: ' +
        right + ' / ' + total + '</span>';
      $('og-feedback').innerHTML =
        '<button onclick="window.ogRestart()" ' +
        'style="padding:6px 14px; font-size:14px;">Restart</button>';
      setButtonsDisabled(true);
      return;
    }
    $('og-msg').style.display = 'none';
    $('og-img').style.display = 'block';
    $('og-img').src = items[i].img;
    $('og-img').alt = 'Chart ' + (i + 1);
    $('og-feedback').innerHTML = '';
    setButtonsDisabled(false);
    locked = false;
  }

  window.ogGuess = function (k) {
    if (locked || i >= items.length) return;
    locked = true; total++;
    const ok = (k === items[i].k); if (ok) right++;
    $('og-score').textContent = 'Score: ' + right + ' / ' + total;
    $('og-feedback').innerHTML =
      (ok ? '✅ Correct' : '❌ Wrong') +
      ' — <em>' + labelFor(items[i].k) + '</em>' +
      ' <button onclick="window.ogNext()" ' +
      'style="margin-left:12px; padding:6px 14px; font-size:14px;">Next →</button>';
    setButtonsDisabled(true);
  };

  window.ogNext    = function () { i++; render(); };

  window.ogRestart = function () {
    i = 0; right = 0; total = 0;
    shuffle(items);
    $('og-score').textContent = 'Score: 0 / 0';
    render();
  };

  if (!items.length || !outlets.length) {
    $('og-msg').innerHTML =
      '<span style="color:#C2001A;">No outlet screenshots embedded.</span><br>' +
      '<span style="font-size:14px; color:#888;">Drop PNG/JPG files into ' +
      '<code>app/</code> (filename = outlet key, e.g. <code>ft.png</code>) ' +
      'and re-knit.</span>';
    return;
  }

  renderButtons();
  shuffle(items);
  render();
})();
</script>

# House styles

.pull-left[
## What is a house style?

A house style is *internally consistent* and *externally
recognisable*. Both matter.

## Tools are not neutral

Every tool encodes assumptions about what is *normal*:

- `ggplot2`'s grey panel and serif title: "this is a plot for analysts".
- Excel's pastel gradient: corporate-meeting-coded.
- Datawrapper's blue–orange diverging: newsroom-neutral, but it *is* a choice.

Each of these encodes who the chart is *for*. Choosing them passively
is choosing — you just didn't know you were choosing.
]

.pull-right[
## What this means for you

You don't have a house style — *yet*. But every chart you publish is
training your audience to expect one. So:

1. Pick a small, fixed palette (3–5 colours, plus grey for "context"
   data) and stick to it across pieces.
2. Pick *one* font and use it everywhere. Default sans is fine.
3. Decide once: do your titles end in a period? Do your axis labels
   include units? Where does the source line live?
4. Write a `theme_yourname()` and reuse it.
]



---
# Don't reinvent the wheel — start from a base theme

.pull-left[
## Built into ggplot2

`theme_grey()` *(default)*, `theme_bw()`, `theme_minimal()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_void()`, `theme_dark()`, `theme_light()`.

```{r theme-base-demo, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()        #<<
```

## Pre-baked publication looks: `ggthemes`

```{r theme-ggthemes-install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("ggthemes")
library(ggthemes)
```

You get `theme_economist()`, `theme_fivethirtyeight()`, `theme_wsj()`, `theme_stata()`, `theme_excel_new()`, `theme_tufte()`, `theme_few()`, ... — each modelled on a real outlet's house style. I recommend none of them.
]

.pull-right[
## Why bother with a base?

A base theme decides **80%** of the boring stuff for you — panel
background, axis lines, gridlines, default font sizes — so you can
focus on the **20%** that's editorial: palette, type, annotation
placement.

## A common workflow

1. Pick a base (`theme_minimal()` is a good neutral starting point).
2. Override the few elements that matter for *your* style (`theme(...)`).
3. Save the combination as `theme_yourname()`.
4. Re-use across every chart in a project.
]



---
# Same plot, four `ggthemes`

```{r ggthemes-compare, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.6, dpi=150, out.width="100%"}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
library(patchwork)

base_p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title    = "Engine size vs. highway mpg",
    subtitle = "By cylinder count",
    caption  = "Source: EPA fueleconomy.gov",
    x = "Displacement (L)", y = "Highway mpg",
    colour = "cyl"
  )

p_excel <- base_p + theme_excel_new(base_size = 9) +
  ggtitle("theme_excel_new()")
p_538   <- base_p + theme_fivethirtyeight(base_size = 9) +
  ggtitle("theme_fivethirtyeight()")
p_stata <- base_p + theme_stata(base_size = 9) +
  scale_colour_stata() +
  ggtitle("theme_stata()")
p_wsj   <- base_p + theme_wsj(base_size = 9) +
  scale_colour_wsj() +
  ggtitle("theme_wsj()")

(p_excel + p_538) / (p_stata + p_wsj)
```


---
# Roll your own `theme_yourname()`

.pull-left[
A custom theme is just a function that returns a `theme()` object on
top of a base.

```{r theme-yourname, eval=FALSE}
theme_dj <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title.position   = "plot",
      plot.title            = element_text(
        face = "bold", size = rel(1.15),
        margin = margin(b = 4)),
      plot.subtitle         = element_text(
        colour = "grey30",
        margin = margin(b = 14)),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      plot.caption          = element_text(
        colour = "grey45", hjust = 0,
        size = rel(0.7),
        margin = margin(t = 12)),
      panel.grid.minor      = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x    = element_blank(),
      axis.text             = element_text(colour = "grey30")
    )
}
```
]

.pull-right[
## Your theme in action

```{r theme-yourname-use, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title    = "Bigger engines, lower mileage",
       subtitle = "EPA fuel-economy data, 1999–2008",
       caption  = "Source: EPA fueleconomy.gov") +
  theme_dj()                        #<<
```

## Two patterns worth stealing

- Use `rel()` for sizes so everything scales when you change `base_size`.
- Set `plot.title.position = "plot"` so the title and caption align with the plot edges, not the panel — a small detail readers feel without naming.

Once your theme is stable, drop it in a tiny `R/theme_dj.R` and `source()` it from every report. Same `theme_dj()`, every chart.
]

# 3. Interactivity has to earn its place
<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px style="width:1000px; margin:auto;"/></html>



---
# Most readers do not interact

.pull-left[
## What the research and newsroom analytics find

- **Boy, Détienne & Fekete (CHI 2015)** ran three field experiments on a major news site and a viz gallery: introductory "story" framing on an interactive chart **did not** increase subsequent exploration. ([HAL preprint](https://inria.hal.science/hal-01133305/) · [ACM](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2702123.2702452))

- **Archie Tse, NYT (Malofiej 2016)** — "Why we are doing fewer interactives". Internal NYT data: most clickable elements got <10% engagement. ([Nieman Lab summary](https://www.niemanlab.org/2016/03/at-the-malofiej-infographics-world-summit-the-best-form-of-storytelling-is-often-static/) · [slides](https://github.com/archietse/malofiej-2016))

- **Gregor Aisch, NYT (2017)** — pushes back, but confirms the underlying number: **~85% of readers** of NYT graphics from 2015 did not click any button. ([In Defense of Interactive Graphics](http://www.vis4.net/blog/in-defense-of-interactive-graphics/))
]

.pull-right[
<br>

---
# Default to static.

.pull-left-small2[
## 3 rules for visual storytelling

1. If you make the reader click or do anything other than scroll, something spectacular has to happen.
2. If you make a tooltip or rollover, assume no one will ever see it. If content is important for readers to see, don't hide it.
3. When deciding whether to make something interactive, remember that getting it to work on all platforms is expensive.

By [Archie Tse, NYT](https://github.com/archietse/malofiej-2016), 2016
]

.pull-right-wide2[
## Case study
<div align="center">
<img src="pics/upshot-immigrants-1.png" style="width:75%; height:auto;">

.center[`Source` [Anna Flagg for NYT The Upshot](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/03/30/upshot/crime-immigration-myth.html)
]
]


---
# Scrollytelling is the right ceiling, often

.pull-left-small[
## Good scrollytelling

Scrolling is *also* an interaction — but it is the one your reader is
already doing.

- one chart that **transforms** as you scroll,
- annotations that **arrive** at the right moment,
- never asks the reader to *do* anything except keep going.

This pattern carries the narrative without the cognitive overhead of
filters, dropdowns, or dragging.
]

# 4. Build for the phone first
<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px style="width:1000px; margin:auto;"/></html>



---
# Where your readers actually are

.pull-left[
## Some evidence 
- **Mobile is now the dominant news channel.** Reuters Institute *Digital News Report 2025* finds smartphones the most-used news device in most markets surveyed. ([report](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025))
- **In the US, 86%** of adults get news at least sometimes from a smartphone, tablet, or computer; **21%** prefer apps and websites over any other source. (Pew Research, *News Platform Fact Sheet*, 2025 — [link](https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/news-platform-fact-sheet/))
- The mobile viewport width of [common smartphones](https://yesviz.com/iphones.php) is **~400px wide**. Your typical reader sees the chart smaller than your laptop preview.

> A one-row, four-panel small-multiples chart that shines on a 27" monitor *dies* on a 390px column. Designing for desktop and "just hoping mobile works" is the modern equivalent of designing for print and assuming the website will be fine.
]

.pull-right[
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; align-items:flex-start; gap:16px;">
  <video src="pics/datawrapper-mobile.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline
         style="width:100%; max-height:480px; object-fit:contain;"></video>
</div>

.center[
`Source` [Datawrapper](https://www.datawrapper.de/academy/locator-maps-for-mobile-devices)
]
]


---
# Implications for your work

.pull-left[

## One chart, one finding.

In that sense, mobile forces a discipline on you. If you have three findings, you have three charts. Stop combining too much into one chart.

## A mobile sanity check before you publish

1. Open the live page on your phone.
2. Read it with your phone held normally — not zoomed in.
3. Can you read every label? Can you tell what the headline finding is in 5 seconds?
4. If you are using ggplot, render at `width = 4, height = 5, dpi = 300` and look at it small.

Browser extensions like `Mobile simulator` let you emulate the mobile ezperience on desktop. If anything fails: cut a series, raise the type size, redo the title.
]

.pull-right[
## What "mobile-first" actually changes

| Feature | Desktop | Mobile |
|---|---|---|
| Aspect ratio | landscape (16:9) | portrait or square |
| Series in one chart | up to ~6 | 1–2; rest go to small multiples or get cut |
| Type size | 11–12pt | 14–16pt minimum |
| Legend | OK | direct labels only |
| Title | one line | wraps to 2–3 lines |
| Axis labels | full text | abbreviated or removed |
| Small multiples | grid (e.g. 4×4) | 1-column stack |
| Interactivity | hover tooltips | tap-and-hold; usually drop |
]

---
class: exercise
# Workshop II — design a chart on the whiteboard

.pull-left[
## The brief
The **V-Dem Institute's 2024 release** shows the global
electoral democracy index has fallen back to **1986 levels**. But the
global average masks dramatic divergence: large democracies have
backslid (US, India, Brazil under Bolsonaro), a handful of autocracies
have liberalized, and entire regions move in opposite directions
within the same decade.

You have **10 minutes**, in teams of 3–4, to **sketch one chart on
the whiteboard** for a piece on this. No laptops.

## Constraints

- **One chart only.**
- It can be **static or interactive.**

We'll walk around at the end.
]

.pull-right[
## The dataset — V-Dem v14, country-year panel

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `country` | chr | ~180 countries |
| `year` | int | 1990 – 2023 |
| `region` | chr | 10 world regions |
| `v2x_polyarchy` | dbl | Electoral Democracy Index, 0–1 |
| `regime_type` | chr | Closed autocracy → Liberal democracy (4 cats) |
| `population` | dbl | Total population, optional weight |

**Shape:** ~180 countries × 34 years ≈ **6,100 country-year rows.**

<br>

`Source` [V-Dem Institute, *Varieties of Democracy*](https://v-dem.net/data/the-v-dem-dataset/) · [Democracy Report 2024](https://v-dem.net/publications/democracy-reports/)
]

# Your charts: live discussion

---
class: exercise
# Your submitted charts

.pull-left[
A few of you volunteered charts from your own data-bit and other works. We'll go
through them one by one. For each, the room will:

1. **Read it cold.** What's the headline finding? (no help from the author)
2. **Spot the editorial choices.** What was foregrounded? What was cut?
3. **Provide constructive feedback.** Where does it shine? Where would we change it?
4. **Author's reply.** What did you mean to say, and did the chart say it?

The goal isn't to praise or pile on. It's to practise the act of
*reading* a chart with the same care we apply to writing one.
]

# Further reading

**Books**
- Claus Wilke, [*Fundamentals of Data Visualization*](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/) — a standard reference.
- Alberto Cairo, [*The Truthful Art*](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/the-truthful-art/9780133440492/) and [*How Charts Lie*](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324001560) — both written for practitioners.
- Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, [*Storytelling with Data: Let's Practice!*](https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/letspractice/downloads) — workshop-style, you're probably beyond this.

**Blogs / Newsletters / Online material**
- [Datawrapper Blog](https://www.datawrapper.de/blog) — Lisa Charlotte Muth's *Data Vis Dispatch* is the single best weekly digest.
- [Junk Charts](https://www.junkcharts.com/) — Kaiser Fung's redesigns.
- [Open Visualization Academy](https://openvisualizationacademy.org/) — Free courses by Alberto Cairo and others.
- [The Functional Art](http://www.thefunctionalart.com/) — Alberto Cairo.

**Newsroom showcases**
- [FT Visual Vocabulary](https://ft-interactive.github.io/visual-vocabulary/)
- [Reuters Graphics](https://www.reuters.com/graphics/) | [Pudding](https://pudding.cool/) | [NYT Upshot](https://www.nytimes.com/section/upshot)
- [Sigma Awards](https://www.sigmaawards.org/) — annual data-journalism prize
